topic: Defining the coach's role in skills work
stem: A collegiate women's soccer coach hires a consultant for weekly 30-minute team sessions during preseason. At the planning meeting she says, 'The mental side is your area, so I'll stay out of it and run practice as usual.' Assessment shows players want a quick reset after mistakes, and the consultant will not attend the daily practices where the reset would be rehearsed. What is the best response to the coach?
options: Accept her plan, so that players see the sessions as a space kept apart from selection decisions
Ask her to lead the team sessions herself after a briefing, with the consultant advising in the background
Suggest a small, defined coach role, such as prompting the team's reset cue during practice drills
Agree to her plan for preseason, and revisit the coach's role once the players know the skills
rationales: Keeping sessions apart from selection is a reasonable aim, but it does not require the coach to stay out entirely. Without her involvement, the reset is never prompted in practice, where players most need it.
Handing delivery to the coach shifts the consultant's own role onto her before she has the knowledge or the wish to take it on, and it is not what she asked for.

Mental skills transfer when they are reinforced in the training environment, and coaches are the people present when that happens. Agreeing on a small, defined coach role at the outset clarifies who does what and links the sessions to practice without turning the coach into the consultant.
Roles are easiest to set at the start; waiting until the skills are learned lets a separation take hold that leaves the reset unrehearsed in practice during the weeks it is being learned.
takeaway: Clarify early how the coach will reinforce skills in practice; a small, defined coach role links sessions to the training environment.

stem: At an intake meeting, Haruto, an elite golfer, says, 'I'll show up every week and you can tell me what's wrong with my head, the same way my swing coach fixes my mechanics.' How should the consultant describe the way they will work together?
options: Each step will be decided jointly, drawing on what he already knows about his own game
The consultant will assess his mental game first, then prescribe a plan for him to follow
They will begin weekly sessions as he suggests, and discuss working style once rapport builds
They will agree on goals together, and the consultant will then supply a technique to fix each
rationales: Mental performance work is collaborative and educational: the client is the expert on his own experience and an active partner in choosing and practicing skills, while the consultant contributes knowledge and structure. Describing that partnership at intake shapes the working alliance and his ownership of the plan.
Assessment does come early, but presenting the consultant as the expert who diagnoses and prescribes accepts the 'fix me' model he described and casts him as a passive recipient.
Expectations about roles are best set at the outset. Starting on his terms and discussing them later lets the passive model he described become the pattern.
Agreeing on goals together is a good start, but having the consultant then supply a fix for each one keeps the 'fix me' model he described and leaves him a passive recipient of corrections.
takeaway: At intake, describe mental performance work as a partnership in which the client's knowledge shapes the plan, not as corrections from an expert.

topic: Realistic outcomes of a one-off workshop
stem: The vice president of a logistics company asks a consultant to run a single 90-minute 'resilience workshop' for 200 employees. She says she expects the company's burnout survey scores to drop by next quarter. Before agreeing, what should the consultant clarify with her first?
options: Which burnout survey the company uses, and when it could be repeated to track the change
Whether attendance will be voluntary, so employees can choose whether to take part
Whether she will fund follow-up sessions if the first workshop lowers the burnout scores
What one workshop can realistically change, and what follow-up her goal would require
rationales: Choosing a measure matters, but it is premature while the expected outcome itself is unrealistic; agreeing on objectives comes before deciding how to evaluate them.

Voluntary participation is a fair question to settle, but it can wait until the purpose of the work is agreed, and it does not address the mismatch between one workshop and her expected drop in burnout.
This builds on the assumption that one workshop will lower burnout, which is the very expectation the consultant needs to correct before committing.

A single psychoeducational session can raise awareness and introduce skills, but it is unlikely by itself to shift burnout, which also reflects workload and organizational conditions. Aligning on realistic objectives and the follow-up and supports they would require comes first in organizational work.
takeaway: In organizational work, align on what the format can realistically achieve before agreeing to deliver or measure it.

stem: A high school athletic director plans to offer mental performance training only to 'athletes who are struggling or have problems.' He worries that offering it to everyone will suggest something is wrong with them. Which explanation best describes what mental performance training is?
options: A support service for athletes facing setbacks, so offering it when they struggle makes sense
Training in learnable skills that help any performer, much as strength and conditioning does
An extension of coaching that works best for athletes already performing at a high level
A wellness resource that pairs with counseling, so it is best offered through that service
rationales: Mental skills can help athletes who are struggling, but framing the service as a response to setbacks makes it reactive and reinforces the idea that using it means something is wrong.

Mental performance training is educational and skills-based: abilities such as goal setting, focus, and arousal regulation are learnable and help performers at every level, just as physical training does. Framing it this way also reduces the stigma the director is worried about.
Skills training benefits developing and struggling performers as well as top ones; tying it to athletes who already excel misreads what the training is for.
Counseling addresses mental health concerns and is delivered by licensed professionals. Linking skills training to it confuses the two services and adds to the stigma the director wants to avoid.
takeaway: Mental performance training is skill education for all performers, not therapy and not a crisis response.

stem: A professional volleyball club hires a consultant for six hours per month. The head coach expects the consultant to design and deliver an individualized mental performance plan for each of the 18 players on the roster. What should the consultant do first?
options: Accept the expectation, and shorten each player's sessions so that 18 plans fit the contract
Ask the club to discuss a larger contract, since 18 individualized plans need more hours
Discuss which needs suit team sessions and how individual time will work, then agree a model
Interview each player first, then decide with the coach who most needs an individual plan
rationales: Spreading six hours across 18 individualized plans leaves too little contact for any of them to work, so agreeing to it sets up a program that cannot deliver what was promised.
More hours might help, but opening with a request for a bigger contract skips the conversation about what can realistically be delivered within the current one.

Clarifying the delivery model with the coach at the outset, including which needs are best met in team sessions and how individual work will be offered within the hours available, aligns expectations with resources before services begin.
Interviewing every player is itself a large share of the limited hours and starts the work before the coach and consultant agree on what the service will look like.
takeaway: Before starting team work, agree with the coach on what team versus individual delivery can realistically cover in the time available.

stem: Isabela, a professional violist preparing for orchestra auditions, tells a consultant at their first meeting, 'I want you to make my nerves go away completely, so I never feel them on stage again.' Which response best sets accurate expectations for the work?
options: Accept the goal, and begin relaxation training so her arousal is lower before each audition
Explain that nerves tend to fade with audition experience, so the work will center on mock auditions
Suggest she ask her physician about beta-blockers, which many orchestral players use for auditions
Explain that the aim is to manage and interpret nerves so they interfere less, not remove them
rationales: Relaxation skills may help, but accepting a goal of never feeling nerves sets an unattainable target and may lead her to treat any nervousness as failure. Some arousal before a high-stakes performance is normal and can be useful.

Mock auditions are a useful way to practice under pressure, but promising that nerves will fade still makes their absence the target and leaves out how she interprets the symptoms she will still feel.
Medication is a medical decision outside the consultant's role, and nothing in her request suggests a medical concern; raising it first sidesteps the expectation-setting she needs.

Mental performance training helps performers regulate arousal and reinterpret symptoms; research on directional interpretation shows the same symptoms can be experienced as facilitative. Setting the goal as managing nerves rather than removing them is realistic and motivating.
takeaway: Set the goal as managing and reinterpreting nerves, not eliminating them.

stem: A collegiate men's basketball coach invites the team's consultant to travel to the conference tournament and suggests the consultant sit on the bench and 'give the guys a mental boost' during timeouts. Players have practiced a breathing-and-cue reset with the consultant all season, and timeouts are when the staff gives tactical instructions. Which role should the consultant propose for the tournament?
options: Stay in the background at the venue, prompting the reset players already use when they want it
Lead a short focus exercise during each timeout, planned with the head coach before every game
Introduce a new pre-game visualization for the tournament, while keeping the bench to the staff
Offer support by phone from home, so the bench stays clearly within the coaching staff's domain
rationales: At competitions the consultant's role is usually low-profile: supporting routines athletes have already learned and being available, without competing with coaches for players' attention at tactical moments. Agreeing on that role before travel prevents confusion on site.
Timeouts belong to tactical instruction; adding an exercise there competes with the coaches and adds a new demand at a critical moment, even if it is planned in advance.
The team already has a practiced reset, and a technique first tried at a tournament is unlikely to be dependable when it counts.
Remote support is an option, but the coach invited the consultant on site, and a low-key presence at the venue can respect the staff's role while keeping support close at hand.
takeaway: At competitions, support routines athletes already use and stay out of the coaches' tactical moments.

stem: A parent books mental performance sessions for Anselm, a 14-year-old figure skater, hoping to improve his consistency in competition. At the first meeting, Anselm shrugs and says he is only there because his mother made him come. What should the consultant explain to Anselm and his parent?
options: Sessions will go ahead as planned, since his mother's permission covers training for a minor
The work depends on Anselm's involvement, so they will start with his goals and seek his assent
The consultant will meet his mother first to agree on goals, then bring Anselm into the process
Anselm can take a few weeks to decide whether to continue, with sessions paused until he chooses
rationales: A guardian's permission is required for a minor, but it does not make the training effective, and the minor's assent is also expected; skills develop only if the athlete engages.

Mental skills are learned through the performer's active practice, so progress depends on Anselm's engagement. Exploring his own goals and seeking his assent, alongside the parent's permission, sets realistic expectations for both and gives the work a chance to succeed.
The parent's hopes matter, but setting goals with her before hearing from Anselm repeats the arrangement that made him reluctant and sidelines his assent.
Giving him time respects his autonomy, but pausing skips the chance to find out whether he has goals of his own; initial reluctance is common and often shifts once those are explored.
takeaway: When someone else arranges the work, explain that progress depends on the performer's own engagement and seek a minor's assent.

topic: Scope when asked to plan training
stem: Gwen, a 52-year-old triathlete who meets a consultant by video, has no coach and trains from online plans. After several sessions on race-day focus, she asks the consultant to also write her weekly training schedule and taper for her next race, saying, 'You already know how stress affects me.' The consultant has no training in exercise programming. How should the consultant respond?
options: Draft a light taper only, since recovery and stress are closely tied to her mental readiness
Write the plan, and ask her to have her physician review it before she begins following it
Cover training loads in their sessions, noting that the advice reflects a mental-skills viewpoint
Suggest a qualified triathlon coach for the plan, and offer to fit race-day routines to it
rationales: A taper is a training prescription, so drafting even a light one moves outside the consultant's competence, however closely recovery and stress are linked.
A physician's review does not turn the consultant into a qualified programmer; it adds a check but leaves the consultant prescribing training outside their competence.
Labeling the advice as coming from a mental-skills viewpoint does not change that it is training prescription outside the consultant's competence.

Practicing within one's competence means leaving exercise programming to qualified coaches. The consultant can still serve her well by pointing her to a qualified coach and, with her consent, coordinating so her race-day mental routines fit the taper that coach designs.
takeaway: When asked for training programming, connect the performer with a qualified coach and coordinate the mental plan around it.

stem: A fire chief hires a consultant to deliver mental performance training to all firefighters in the department. He also asks the consultant to use the sessions to identify which firefighters are 'mentally weak' so he can consider reassigning them, adding that he is open to suggestions about how the program should run. What should the consultant do?
options: Agree to share observations, so long as firefighters are told at the start that the chief will see them
Offer a separate formal assessment for staffing, then run the training purely as a skills program
Clarify that the program builds skills rather than rating people, and agree on what is reported
Decline the contract, since a dual purpose would compromise the firefighters' trust from the outset
rationales: Telling participants is better than hidden screening, but it still turns skills sessions into an evaluation that they were never designed to provide, and it discourages the honest engagement the training depends on.

Personnel screening is a different service that requires validated methods and competence for selection decisions; proposing it shifts the consultant into a role the chief's real need may not require.

In organizational work, the consultant clarifies at the outset who the client is, what the service is for, and what information will be shared. Framing the program as skill development and agreeing on reporting that participants know about protects trust and keeps the training effective.
The concern is valid, but the chief has said he is open to suggestions, so declining before clarifying the program's purpose and reporting is premature.
takeaway: Agree with organizational sponsors on the program's purpose and on what will be reported before delivery begins.

stem: Bastian, a collegiate tennis player, says he 'loses focus' in matches even though he trains well. Before planning any intervention, the consultant wants a questionnaire showing how often he already uses a range of psychological strategies, such as self-talk, imagery, and activation control, and how that use differs between matches and training. Which instrument best fits this purpose?
options: Athletic Coping Skills Inventory-28 (ACSI-28)
Test of Performance Strategies (TOPS)
Sport Imagery Questionnaire (SIQ)
Test of Attentional and Interpersonal Style (TAIS)
rationales: The ACSI-28 measures broad psychological coping skills, such as concentration and coping with adversity, but it does not record how often specific strategies are used or compare practice with competition.

The TOPS assesses how often athletes use psychological strategies, such as self-talk, imagery, relaxation, activation, goal setting, and attentional control, with separate practice and competition scales. That makes it well suited to mapping current strategy use before planning.
The SIQ measures how often athletes use imagery for different functions, but it covers imagery alone rather than the range of strategies the consultant wants to map.
The TAIS describes attentional and interpersonal style, which relates to his focus complaint, but it does not show which strategies he uses in matches and training.
takeaway: To map how often a performer uses a range of mental strategies in practice and competition, the TOPS fits; coping, imagery, and attention measures answer narrower questions.

stem: A consultant who has worked mainly with hockey skaters agrees to help Petra, a 16-year-old ice hockey goaltender who says she 'falls apart' after letting in a soft goal. The consultant knows little about how goaltending differs mentally from skating positions. Before deciding what to assess in Petra herself, which step best informs the assessment plan?
options: Give Petra the ACSI-28 to build a broad profile of her coping skills before the next game
Run the intake interview used with skaters, then adapt it once Petra's answers come in
Have Petra log each soft goal and her reactions to it over the next three games
Observe her games and interview the goalie coach about the position's psychological demands
rationales: A coping-skills inventory gives a general profile of Petra, but the consultant does not yet know which skills matter most in goaltending, so the results would be hard to interpret.

A standard intake interview is a sensible start with most clients, but questions built for skaters may miss what is distinctive about the position, and adapting afterward puts the step in the wrong order.
Self-monitoring can provide useful data later, but it assesses Petra before the consultant understands what the position asks of her, so it is hard to know what to have her log and why.

When the consultant is unfamiliar with a role, a demands analysis comes first: observing the performance setting and consulting an expert, such as the position coach, shows when focus, recovery, and emotional control matter most. That knowledge then guides which skills to assess in the athlete.
takeaway: When a role is unfamiliar, analyze its psychological demands through observation and expert input before choosing what to assess in the performer.

stem: A consultant is planning imagery training for Ama, a collegiate pole vaulter who says she 'can't really picture or feel' her jumps when she tries to imagine them. Before designing the program, the consultant wants to measure how easily Ama can form visual and kinesthetic images of her jumps. Which instrument best fits this purpose?
options: Movement Imagery Questionnaire-3 (MIQ-3)
Sport Imagery Questionnaire (SIQ)
Test of Attentional and Interpersonal Style (TAIS)
Test of Performance Strategies (TOPS)
rationales: The MIQ-3 measures imagery ability, meaning the ease of generating internal visual, external visual, and kinesthetic images, which is exactly what the consultant wants to know before designing the program.
The SIQ measures how often athletes use imagery for its cognitive and motivational functions. It describes frequency of use, not how easily she can form images.
The TAIS assesses attentional and interpersonal style; vivid imagery draws on attention, but the instrument does not measure imagery ability.
The TOPS includes an imagery scale, but it records how often imagery is used in practice and competition, not how easily she can form visual and kinesthetic images.
takeaway: Imagery ability (MIQ-3) and imagery use (SIQ, TOPS) are different questions; pick the measure that matches what you need to know.

stem: Junho, a professional esports player referred by his team's coach, meets a consultant by video. He says, 'I guess mental training could help me in clutch rounds, but I'm not sure it's worth the time with our scrim schedule.' Which response best fits his readiness for mental performance training?
options: Agree on a full daily practice schedule with him, so early results build his commitment
Ask the coach how committed he seems, and plan the program around that report
Explore what he would gain and what it would cost him, then let him choose a first step
Share research on mental training in esports, then invite his questions about the fit
rationales: Junho is ambivalent, not committed; a demanding schedule, even one agreed with him, ignores the time concern he raised and is likely to increase resistance.
The coach's view is secondhand, and planning around it bypasses Junho's own ambivalence, which is what readiness depends on.

His statement fits contemplation: he sees possible benefits but doubts the cost. Exploring both sides of his ambivalence, as in motivational interviewing, and letting him choose a small first step respects his autonomy and moves readiness forward.
Information can help later, but leading with the case for change tends to prompt an ambivalent person to defend the other side. Exploring his own reasons first is more effective at this stage.
takeaway: Match the response to readiness: explore ambivalence and let the performer choose a small first step.

stem: During scenario-based training, a SWAT officer insists that he 'stays calm' under stress, yet instructors notice that his hands shake and his radio calls speed up. The consultant wants to assess his stress response in a way that also builds his self-awareness. Which approach best fits?
options: Interview him in depth about his stress experience, exploring the situations he finds hardest
Pair heart-rate monitoring in scenarios with a debrief comparing the data to his own ratings
Give him a validated trait anxiety questionnaire, and discuss his scores with him afterward
Have instructors share their observations after each scenario, framed as constructive feedback
rationales: An in-depth interview is useful, but it relies on his own account, which conflicts with what observers see and suggests limited awareness of his stress response.

Objective physiological data gathered in realistic scenarios, reviewed with him alongside his own ratings, lets him notice the gap between what he feels and what his body does. That builds self-awareness, and the multi-method data also inform planning.
A validated questionnaire still depends on the same self-perception that seems inaccurate here, and a trait score says little about his responses in the moment.
Outside feedback, however constructive, is another view he can dispute; it does not help him learn to recognize his own signals during scenarios.
takeaway: When self-report and observation disagree, objective data reviewed with the performer can build self-awareness.

stem: Solveig, a collegiate water polo player, scores high on the concentration subscale of the Athletic Coping Skills Inventory-28. Her coach, however, reports that she often loses track of her defensive assignment late in close games. What should the consultant do next?
options: Explore the gap by interviewing Solveig and observing the situations the coach describes
Treat the inventory score as primary, since it is standardized, and discuss that view with the coach
Weight the coach's report more heavily, since self-ratings tend to be favorable
Begin concentration training, and track whether the coach still sees lapses over the next month
rationales: Good assessment is multi-method. When a questionnaire and a stakeholder report disagree, interviewing the athlete and observing the specific situations helps explain the gap, for example fatigue or game pressure rather than general concentration.
Questionnaires capture general self-perceptions and can miss situation-specific problems, so the coach's report should not be set aside, however the view is shared.
Coach reports are also only one perspective. Assuming the athlete's rating is inflated skips the step of finding out what is actually happening.

Monitoring is useful, but starting an intervention before understanding the discrepancy risks targeting the wrong problem; the lapses could reflect fatigue, tactics, or pressure rather than a concentration skill gap.
takeaway: When data sources disagree, gather more information in context rather than choosing one source.

stem: The head coach of a collegiate women's rowing team asks a consultant to run a team-building retreat because the boat 'doesn't feel like a team this year.' The consultant has not yet met the athletes. Which step should come first?
options: Plan an outdoor challenge retreat, then debrief what it shows about how the crew works together
Schedule a social evening so the rowers can reconnect before the next training block begins
Ask the captains to name the main sources of tension so the retreat can address them
Assess task and social cohesion with a questionnaire and interviews with athletes and staff
rationales: Debriefing helps, but choosing the activity before understanding the problem is premature, and adventure activities do not by themselves reliably improve cohesion.
A social event assumes the issue is social cohesion; the problem might instead be task cohesion, such as unclear roles or goals.
Captains' views are useful input, but relying on two athletes gives a narrow picture and still assumes a retreat is the answer before the group has been assessed.

Team building should follow assessment. Measuring task and social cohesion, for example with the Group Environment Questionnaire plus interviews, shows which aspects of cohesion are weak so the intervention can be targeted.
takeaway: Assess task and social cohesion before choosing a team-building intervention.

topic: Checking practice before judging a skill
stem: Six weeks into an imagery plan to improve her composure in juried recitals, Anjali, a collegiate pianist, reports no change in her performances. Her practice log shows she completed imagery twice in six weeks, although she had agreed to four short sessions per week. She says that on the two occasions she did it, the imagery felt vivid and calming. What should the consultant do next?
options: Explore with her what has blocked practice, and revise the plan so it fits her schedule
Switch to a cue-word strategy, and check after two recitals whether it is easier to use
Agree with her on a fixed daily practice time, and keep the imagery plan otherwise unchanged
Discuss whether low follow-through reflects a broader concern that a counselor should assess
rationales: Monitoring has to check whether the skill was actually practiced before judging whether it works. Exploring the barriers with her and adjusting the dose or format to fit her schedule addresses the real problem.
Imagery has barely been tested and seemed to help when she used it; switching techniques without understanding why practice did not happen may leave the same barrier in place.
A fixed time may help some performers, but setting it before learning what blocked practice keeps a dose that has not fit her life and may not address the barrier.
Missing practice is common and does not by itself suggest a clinical concern; nothing in the scenario points outside the consultant's scope.
takeaway: Before deciding an intervention isn't working, check whether it was actually used, and adjust the plan to remove barriers.

stem: Corwin, a collegiate swimmer, set a weekly goal of hitting a target stroke rate on every set. After four weeks he has met it only once and says he feels discouraged, although his stroke rate has improved steadily and is still short of the target. What is the most appropriate adjustment?
options: Replace the stroke-rate goal with a race-time goal, which links his work more clearly to results
Keep the target, and discuss with him how persisting through setbacks builds his resilience
Revise it with him to a challenging but attainable target that steps toward the original
Set an effort goal of completing each set, then return to stroke rate once his confidence lifts
rationales: Race times depend on many factors and would remove the specific process focus that is producing steady improvement.
Talking about persistence does not change a target he almost never meets, and repeated failure undermines motivation and confidence.

Goal-setting principles call for goals that are challenging but attainable, reviewed and adjusted based on progress. Setting a stepped target with him keeps the direction, rewards real improvement, and restores a sense of success.
Effort goals are easy to meet but drop the stroke-rate focus that is producing real improvement; adjusting the target's difficulty keeps that focus.
takeaway: When goals are consistently missed despite progress, revise them collaboratively to be challenging but attainable.

stem: After a six-week stress-management program for paramedics, participants rate the sessions highly and pass a quiz on breathing techniques. The agency director now asks whether crews are actually applying the techniques during emergency calls. Which evaluation step best answers her question?
options: Repeat the satisfaction survey with paramedics from other shifts to broaden the sample
Collect self-reports and supervisor observations of technique use during calls
Give a scenario-based knowledge test on when each technique should be used
Compare patient-care quality indicators from before and after the program
rationales: Satisfaction data reflect reactions to the program (Kirkpatrick's first level); a broader sample still says nothing about whether skills are used on the job.

The director's question concerns behavior in the real setting. Gathering data from more than one source on whether crews use the techniques during calls evaluates transfer, which is the behavior level in Kirkpatrick's model.
A scenario-based test shows whether participants know when to use each technique, which is still the learning level, not evidence that they apply it on calls.
Patient-care indicators are results-level outcomes shaped by many factors; they could not show whether crews are using the techniques, which is what the director asked.
takeaway: High satisfaction and knowledge scores don't show transfer; evaluate whether skills are actually used in the performance setting.

topic: Adjusting to the type of anxiety
stem: For four weeks, Emre, an elite judo athlete, has used diaphragmatic breathing before every match, as his log confirms. He says his body now feels calm before competing, but the night before each tournament he still spends hours replaying worst-case scenarios. How should the consultant adjust the plan?
options: Lengthen the breathing sessions the night before, since they have already calmed his body
Add progressive muscle relaxation at bedtime to deepen his physical calm before sleep
Add a cognitive strategy, such as restructuring or defusion, aimed at the night-before worry
Replace breathing with imagery of successful matches to build his confidence for the event
rationales: Breathing has already calmed his body; more of the same somatic technique is unlikely to address the worry that remains.
Progressive muscle relaxation is another somatic technique, and he reports no remaining bodily tension; the remaining problem is cognitive.

Monitoring shows the skill is being used and has reduced somatic anxiety, while cognitive anxiety persists. The matching hypothesis suggests targeting cognitive anxiety with cognitive techniques, so adding one while keeping the breathing that works is the best adjustment.
Imagery may support confidence, but dropping breathing discards the part of the plan that is working, and success imagery does not directly target the worry cycle.
takeaway: When monitoring shows one component of anxiety improving but another persisting, add a technique matched to the remaining component.

stem: Kavya, a collegiate distance runner, has one goal for the season: finish in the top three at nationals. Assessment shows that she worries about rivals during races and that her anxiety spikes mid-race whenever she falls behind them. Which goal-setting plan best fits her assessment data?
options: Replace the top-three goal with a goal to do her best, so that results stop driving her worry
Keep the top-three goal, and add rival-based targets for each race that build toward it
Keep the outcome goal for motivation, but center races on pacing and process goals
Set a season goal of a personal-best time, since it depends less on rivals than placing does
rationales: 'Do your best' goals are vague and less effective than specific goals, and dropping the outcome goal removes a source of long-term motivation she values.
Rival-based race targets would intensify her focus on competitors, the very pattern that raises her anxiety.

Outcome goals can motivate, but performance goals (such as split times) and process goals (such as relaxed form or cadence) are more controllable. Research comparing goal types links process goals to better attentional focus, self-efficacy, and control of cognitive anxiety, which fits her in-race pattern.
A time goal is more controllable than placing, but a season target gives her nothing to focus on during a race when she falls behind; in-race process goals address that moment.
takeaway: Pair outcome goals with controllable performance and process goals, especially when outcome focus fuels anxiety.

stem: Assessment shows that Marlon, an elite sprinter, performs best when he feels highly energized. Before his recent races, though, he has felt flat and sluggish, rating his arousal well below his own optimal level, while his ratings of motivation for the season remain high. Which intervention should his plan prioritize?
options: Cognitive restructuring of the worries he has about where he will place in each race
A centering routine in the call room to steady his focus before he steps onto the track
Goal-setting work on race targets to rebuild his drive over the coming training block
Energizing strategies, such as upbeat music, quick breathing, and power cue words
rationales: Nothing in the assessment points to worry; the problem is low activation, so a cognitive anxiety strategy targets the wrong issue.
Centering steadies and narrows attention, which suits over-aroused or distracted performers; it does not raise the low activation he reports.
His motivation is already high, and goal work over a training block would not change how activated he feels in the call room on race day.

His arousal is below his optimal zone, so the plan should raise activation. Energizing techniques are the evidence-informed choice; the IZOF view emphasizes that optimal intensity is individual, and his is high.
takeaway: Not every performer needs to calm down; match the direction of arousal regulation to the person's optimal zone.

stem: In mid-season, a collegiate softball coach offers a consultant 15 minutes of team time each week to help with 'composure after errors.' Observation and interviews show the problem is concentrated in the team's two pitchers, who both ask for help, while position players already use a reset cue the coach introduced last year and recover quickly. Which plan best fits the assessment?
options: Work individually with the two pitchers, keeping team time for needs the roster shares
Teach a new post-error reset to the whole team, so that the pitchers do not feel singled out
Track error recovery for another month before planning, to confirm the pattern holds
Ask the pitching coach to cue the team's existing reset with the pitchers during bullpens
rationales: The plan should match the level of the need the assessment found. Here the problem sits with two players who want help, so individual work fits, and team time is better spent on needs the whole roster shares.
Protecting the pitchers from feeling singled out is considerate, but reteaching a skill most players already use spends team time on a team-level fix for an individual-level problem.
The pattern is already clear from observation and interviews, and both pitchers have asked for help; delaying a month adds little and leaves the problem in place.
Coach reinforcement can help later, but the existing cue has not worked for the pitchers, and handing their skill work to the pitching coach skips the individual help they requested.
takeaway: Match the level of intervention, individual or team, to where the assessment shows the need sits.

stem: A consultant is planning self-talk training for Elena, a recreational adult archer who is relearning her release technique with her coach. She wants cue words to use on practice shots. Based on self-talk research, which type of cue fits this task best?
options: Motivational cues such as 'come on, strong' to build intensity before each practice shot
Instructional cues such as 'smooth release' tied to the technical change she is making
A single mood word such as 'calm' to keep her relaxed as she draws and releases
Confidence statements such as 'I am a good archer' repeated at the start of each end
rationales: Motivational self-talk tends to help more on strength, endurance, and power tasks; a fine-motor technique change benefits more from instructional cues.

Research shows instructional self-talk is especially effective for fine-motor, precision tasks and for learning new technique. A short cue tied to the change she is making directs attention to the key element of the skill.
A calming word may help arousal, but nothing suggests she is tense, and it gives no guidance on the movement she is relearning.
Confidence statements may support mood, but they give no guidance on the specific movement she is trying to learn.
takeaway: Use instructional self-talk for precision and learning tasks, motivational self-talk for strength, endurance, and power.

stem: Leandro, an elite wheelchair racer, will spend three months training abroad and can meet his consultant only by video every two weeks. Together they plan to build a pre-race routine that includes breathing and imagery. Which plan element best supports his skill development between sessions?
options: Using each video session to rehearse the full routine live, so technique is checked every two weeks
Providing recorded guided practice and a brief log that they review at each video session
Recommending a well-rated meditation app that he can use on days he feels he needs it
Asking his coach abroad to lead the routine with him before races and report back on it
rationales: Live rehearsal during sessions is useful for checking technique, but practice every two weeks gives far too few repetitions for a routine to become reliable.

With infrequent virtual contact, the plan needs structured, independent practice. Recorded guidance tailored to his routine, plus a log reviewed at each session, supports regular practice, accountability, and monitoring.
A general app is not tailored to his routine, and leaving the dose to how he feels provides no structure or way to monitor practice.
The coach has not been trained in the routine, and reporting back raises confidentiality questions; it also shifts the skill work to someone outside the consulting role.
takeaway: With infrequent or virtual contact, build in structured between-session practice and a way to review it.

stem: The coach of a collegiate esports team says the team's goal for the semester is to 'communicate better.' After reviewing match recordings, the consultant notes that players are slow to tell teammates where opponents are. Which revision of the goal best fits goal-setting research?
options: Win at least 70 percent of matches this semester, with communication reviewed after each loss
Speak at least 20 times per round, counted by the coach from each match recording
Raise players' self-rated communication from 3 to 4 on a 5-point scale by midterm
Report 90 percent of enemy sightings within two seconds, tracked weekly in match reviews
rationales: A win-rate target is specific, but it is an outcome goal shaped by many factors beyond communication and does not tell players what to do differently.
A call count is measurable, but it rewards talking more rather than the timely enemy information the consultant observed was missing.
Self-ratings are measurable but subjective, and they do not target the specific behavior seen in the match recordings.
Specific, measurable goals with regular feedback lead to better performance than vague goals. This revision targets the observed problem, sets a clear standard, and builds in a way to track progress.
takeaway: Turn vague goals into specific, measurable versions of the behavior that actually needs to change, with built-in feedback.

stem: Mei, an elite springboard diver, brings her goals for the next training block to her consultant. Each is worded as something to avoid: 'Don't over-rotate the reverse two-and-a-half,' 'Don't look at the judges,' and 'Don't freeze on the board.' She wrote them herself and says she is committed to them. Which revision best fits goal-setting guidance?
options: Reword each as an action to carry out, such as 'spot the water early and kick out on cue'
Add a measurable limit to each, such as no more than one over-rotation in a training session
Keep the wording she chose, since goals an athlete writes herself build commitment
Replace them with one goal of reaching the national final, which keeps her attention forward
rationales: Goal-setting guidance favors positively framed goals that state what to do. Avoidance wording keeps attention on the error, while an action-focused goal directs attention to the cue that produces the skill, and rewording her own goals keeps her ownership.
A numerical limit makes the goal measurable, but it is still framed around the error and keeps her attention on what to avoid.
Ownership supports commitment, but she can keep ownership while rewording; leaving the avoidance framing keeps her attention on mistakes.
An outcome goal may motivate, but it gives her nothing to focus on during a dive and drops the specific technical aims she identified.
takeaway: Frame goals as actions to perform rather than errors to avoid, keeping the performer's ownership of the wording.

stem: A consultant has six weekly one-hour sessions with a high school volleyball team that has never done mental skills training. The coach wants players to have a reliable pre-serve routine by the end. The routine will combine a breath, a cue word, and a brief image of the serve, none of which players have learned. Which sequence best fits an evidence-informed plan?
options: Teach the full pre-serve routine in week one, then refine each of its parts in later weeks
Cover a different mental skill each week, then let players pick which ones to keep in a routine
Teach awareness and the basic skills first, then combine them into a routine practiced in drills
Spend four weeks on goal setting and team values, then build the routine in the last two weeks
rationales: Players cannot run a routine well before they can perform its parts, and these players have learned none of them, so starting with the full routine reverses the logical order.
Sampling many skills may build knowledge, but it spreads six sessions thin and leaves little time to integrate and rehearse the routine the coach wants.

A sound plan moves from education and awareness to basic skills, such as breathing and cue words, then integrates them into a routine practiced in drills. Building from components to integration gives the routine time to become reliable.
Goal setting and values are useful, but leaving two weeks for three new components and their integration is unlikely to produce a reliable routine.
takeaway: Sequence plans from awareness and basic skills to integrated routines, with practice throughout.

stem: Assessment shows that Chiamaka, an elite fencer, avoids starting attacks in close bouts because she fears looking foolish if they fail. She says she wants to be known as a bold, creative fencer. Her consultant is planning an acceptance-based approach. Which plan element best fits that approach?
options: Set committed-action goals to attack in practice bouts while making room for the fear
Build her confidence with mastery imagery of attacks first, then add attacking drills
Teach her to replace fearful thoughts with confident statements before each bout
Lower her anxiety with relaxation training, and reintroduce attacking drills as it eases
rationales: Acceptance-based approaches such as ACT and MAC pair values with committed action: she sets concrete steps toward bold fencing and takes them while willingly experiencing the fear rather than waiting for it to disappear.
Mastery imagery can build confidence, but making attacks wait until she feels confident is a control-first sequence; acceptance-based work has her act on her values with the fear present.
Replacing thoughts is a change-the-content strategy from cognitive approaches; acceptance-based work instead helps her notice fearful thoughts without needing to remove them.
Relaxation skills have a place, but making action wait until anxiety eases keeps the avoidance pattern in charge. Acceptance-based work has her act on her values with the fear present.
takeaway: In acceptance-based plans, committed action toward values happens with discomfort present, not after it is gone.

stem: The coach of an elite women's field hockey team wants every player to follow the same captain-led, 20-minute pre-match mental routine to build team unity. Pre-match ratings over several games show players differ widely: some perform best calm and quiet, others energized and talkative, with many in between. Which plan best fits the assessment?
options: Use one shared routine as the coach proposed, since a common ritual helps build team unity
Let each player design her own routine, and drop the captain-led segment altogether
Split the squad into calm and energized groups, each with its own captain-led routine
Agree on a brief shared team element, followed by time for each player's own preparation
rationales: Shared rituals can support unity, but one 20-minute routine will push some players away from the arousal level at which they perform best.
Individual routines respect personal zones, but removing every shared element gives up the team unity the coach is asking for.
Grouping respects two broad types, but many players fall between them, and splitting the squad works against the unity the coach wants.

The IZOF view holds that optimal pre-performance states are individual. A brief shared element meets the coach's goal of unity, and protected time for individual preparation lets each player reach her own optimal zone.
takeaway: Team routines can combine a short shared element with individual preparation that respects each player's optimal zone.

stem: After several poor outings, Caleb, a collegiate pitcher, says he has lost confidence in his slider. His coach plans to keep telling him he is a great pitcher. According to self-efficacy theory, which strategy should the confidence-building plan emphasize?
options: Daily specific feedback from his pitching coach on what is working in his slider
Watching a teammate of similar ability throw sliders well during bullpen sessions
Graded bullpen tasks that build a record of successful sliders before he uses it in games
Imagery of throwing sharp sliders in game situations, practiced before each outing
rationales: Specific feedback is more useful than general praise, but verbal persuasion is still a weaker source of self-efficacy than his own successful performances.
A similar model makes vicarious experience more useful, but watching someone else succeed is weaker than succeeding himself.

Bandura identified performance accomplishments (mastery experiences) as the strongest source of self-efficacy. Structuring graded tasks he can succeed at gives him direct evidence that he can throw the pitch.
Imagery can contribute to self-efficacy, but imagined success is a weaker source than real, graded successes with the pitch.
takeaway: Mastery experiences are the strongest source of self-efficacy; design graded successes.

stem: A software company's leaders want a mindfulness program to help managers stay focused during high-pressure product launches. HR has already shared research summaries, and managers say they accept the evidence but expect sessions to feel like 'a meditation retreat' with little link to their work. Attendance is voluntary. Which planning choice best fits this group?
options: Open with the history and traditions behind the practices, so managers see where they come from
Present the practices as attention training for launches, with short exercises tied to real tasks
Begin with a detailed review of the research, so managers see why the program merits their time
Run the standard eight-week MBSR curriculum as written, since its outcomes are well documented
rationales: Background on the practices can interest some people, but leading with traditions feeds the very impression of a retreat that is keeping managers from seeing the link to their work.

Planning should adapt content and framing to the population and its goal. Framing mindfulness as attention training for launch pressure, with brief exercises built into real work, addresses their stated concern and makes voluntary practice more likely.
Managers already accept the evidence, so more research does not address their actual concern, which is relevance to their work.
MBSR is well researched, but it was designed for stress reduction in health settings, and delivering it unchanged ignores this group's goal and their concern about relevance.
takeaway: Adapt how a mental skills program is framed and delivered to the group's goals and concerns, not just its evidence base.

stem: A performance profile completed with Sienna, a collegiate dance major, shows large gaps in six areas, from audition nerves to focus in technique class. She has a major audition in ten weeks and little time outside rehearsals. How should the consultant approach planning?
options: Address the six areas in rotation, one per week, so each gets attention before the audition
Choose the two areas the consultant judges most important, and explain the reasoning to her
Invite her to start with the smallest gap, so that an early success builds her momentum
Work with her to choose one or two priorities that matter most for the coming audition
rationales: Rotating through six areas gives each one a single week, too little for any skill to develop with her limited time.
Narrowing the focus is right, but deciding for her, even with reasons, undercuts the ownership that collaborative goal setting builds.
An early win can help motivation, but the smallest gap may not matter for the audition; priority should reflect importance for the upcoming demand, not size alone.
Planning should prioritize collaboratively: a small number of goals chosen with the performer, based on what matters most for the upcoming demand, keeps the plan realistic and builds commitment.
takeaway: Prioritize a few goals together with the client, guided by upcoming demands and time available.

stem: Omar, a professional squash player, and his consultant agree on a goal: using a between-rally refocusing routine to reduce mental lapses after he loses a point. Which plan for measuring progress fits best?
options: Take baseline measures, then track routine use, focus ratings, and points won after errors
Track his match win rate across the season, since it shows whether lapses are costing him
Ask him after each match how well he refocused, and adjust the routine based on his answers
Begin tracking once the routine feels automatic, then compare his first and last months
rationales: A good measurement plan sets a baseline before the intervention and then tracks change repeatedly with several indicators: whether the routine is used, his own ratings of focus, and a performance indicator tied to the goal.
Win rate is a distant outcome shaped by many factors, so it cannot show whether the refocusing routine is working.
Regular check-ins are useful, but relying on one self-report source with no baseline makes it hard to tell whether lapses have actually decreased.
Starting data collection late leaves no baseline to compare against, and problems cannot be caught while the routine is still being learned.
takeaway: Plan measurement up front: baseline, then repeated measures of skill use, process, and performance tied to the goal.

stem: A masters golfer reports that he thinks through his swing mechanics while he is swinging, and his shots have become erratic. His consultant is planning a pre-shot routine using Nideffer's model of attention. Which sequence of attentional focus fits best?
options: Hold a narrow focus on swing mechanics from setup through the finish, to keep technique precise
Scan the course broadly through setup and swing, so that changing conditions stay in view
Read conditions, plan the shot, rehearse its feel, then lock onto a target as he swings
Plan the shot while standing over the ball, then hold a broad view of the hole as he swings
rationales: An internal focus on mechanics during execution is the problem he describes; for skilled performers it tends to disrupt automatic movement.
A broad-external focus suits reading the course, not executing the swing; scanning during the swing pulls attention away from the target.

Nideffer's model describes attention shifting by width and direction. A routine that moves from broad-external (reading conditions) to broad-internal (planning) to narrow-internal (rehearsing the feel), then to a narrow-external target focus, places analysis before the swing and keeps execution free of it.
Separating planning from the swing is right, but a broad view of the hole during the swing is the wrong width; execution calls for a narrow-external focus on a target.
takeaway: Design routines that move attention from broad assessment and planning to brief rehearsal and a narrow-external focus at execution.

stem: A youth soccer club asks a consultant to plan mental skills training for players aged 9 to 11. The coaches can give 15 minutes during each practice. Which plan best fits this population's developmental level?
options: Brief seated talks on positive thinking at the start of practice, with take-home worksheets
Short, active, game-based activities with simple cues that coaches reinforce in practice
Individual goal-setting meetings with each child, held while teammates continue the drill
A shortened version of the club's adult program, in simpler wording for young players
rationales: Talks and worksheets rely on sitting still and abstract reflection, which do not suit children's attention spans or concrete thinking.
Applying research to the population means adapting format and content: children learn best through brief, active, playful activities with concrete cues, reinforced by coaches in everyday practice.
Simple goals can work with children, but one-at-a-time meetings use the 15 minutes on a few players and pull them out of the activity rather than building skills into it.
Adult programs assume abstract reasoning and self-direction that 9- to 11-year-olds are still developing; simpler wording does not fix the mismatch.
takeaway: For children, keep mental skills training short, active, concrete, and woven into practice by coaches.
